discussion_comments.comment_body: Valid, fixed in 8e4ae4f. Added a terminal_kill_all command that the webview calls on load, and the terminal is only offered once that resolves, so a panel restored after the reload cannot have its fresh shell caught by the reap. Verified live: started sleep in a tab, reloaded the webview, the orphaned process was gone and the restored panel came back with a new live shell.

Pushing back. The timeout has to resolve one way, and either direction is "wrong" for one of the two ambiguous cases, so the question is which mistake is cheaper.

For the timeout to fire with no host present, the bus daemon itself has to stall for more than 250 ms: a missing bus fails the connect immediately, and a missing watcher gets ServiceUnknown from dbus-daemon without consulting any other process. A stalled dbus-daemon is not a steady state on any desktop, and if it does happen the result is the pre-existing behavior, which relaunching recovers (the single-instance plugin re-shows the window).

For the timeout to fire with a host present, the watcher (plasmashell, or gnome-shell with the extension) just has to be busy for 250 ms, which is far more plausible. Quitting there ends running sessions on a desktop that has a working tray, and nothing recovers that.

So the timeout deliberately resolves toward hide (ecd266455, after the previous round flagged the other direction). The doc comment on `host_registered_within` records this reasoning.

Not reproducible. `std::process::Child::kill` returns `Ok(())` when the child has already exited (std behavior since Rust 1.72; this crate already needs 1.85+ for `edition2024`), and `wait()` returns the cached status, so retry falls through to `*process = None` and respawns. Checked with the installed toolchain:

```
rustc 1.97.1
try_wait reaped: Some(ExitStatus(unix_wait_status(1792)))
kill() after reap -> Ok(())
wait() after reap -> Ok(ExitStatus(unix_wait_status(1792)))
```

The Windows std impl has the same guard (treats `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` on an exited handle as `Ok`).
